claim: Sympatric timing types of Clunio marinus from Roscoff (France) differ in lunar reproductive timing, with one type reproducing at full moon and the other at new moon.
source: Sympatric timing types of the intertidal insect Clunio marinus (Diptera) from Roscoff (France) differ in lunar reproductive timing. One type reproduces at full moon, the other at new moon, controlled by a circalunar clock of yet unknown molecular nature.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by phenotypic data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Lunar reproductive timing in Clunio marinus is controlled by a circalunar clock of yet unknown molecular nature.
source: One type reproduces at full moon, the other at new moon, controlled by a circalunar clock of yet unknown molecular nature.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is established knowledge about Clunio marinus.

claim: Lunar reproductive timing is a magic trait for a sympatric speciation process because it is both ecologically relevant and entails assortative mating.
source: Lunar reproductive timing is a magic trait for a sympatric speciation process, as it is both ecologically relevant and entails assortative mating.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and explained through inference about the ecological and reproductive consequences of timing differences.

claim: The difference in reproductive timing between FM and NM types is controlled by at least four quantitative trait loci (QTL) on three different chromosomes.
source: Here, we show that the difference in reproductive timing is controlled by at least four quantitative trait loci (QTL) on three different chromosomes.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by QTL mapping data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The QTL controlling reproductive timing are partly associated with complex inversions.
source: They are partly associated with complex inversions, but differentiation of the inversion haplotypes cannot explain the different phenotypes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data showing QTL overlap with inversions in Figures 2 and 5.

claim: Differentiation of the inversion haplotypes cannot explain the different phenotypes in reproductive timing.
source: They are partly associated with complex inversions, but differentiation of the inversion haplotypes cannot explain the different phenotypes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by analysis showing that individual loci are more differentiated than inversions (Figure 5D).

claim: The period locus is the most differentiated locus in the entire genome.
source: The most differentiated locus in the entire genome, with QTL support, is the period locus, implying that this gene could not only be involved in circadian timing but also in lunar timing.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and shown in Figure 5B and 5C with FST values.

claim: The period gene could be involved in both circadian timing and lunar timing.
source: The most differentiated locus in the entire genome, with QTL support, is the period locus, implying that this gene could not only be involved in circadian timing but also in lunar timing.
evidence: This is stated as an implication in the abstract based on the period locus being the most differentiated and overlapping with a QTL.

claim: Magic traits can be based on an oligogenic architecture.
source: Our data indicate that magic traits can be based on an oligogenic architecture and can be maintained by selection on several unlinked loci.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the abstract based on the finding of four unlinked QTL.

claim: Magic traits can be maintained by selection on several unlinked loci.
source: Our data indicate that magic traits can be based on an oligogenic architecture and can be maintained by selection on several unlinked loci.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the abstract based on the QTL mapping results showing unlinked loci.

claim: There is growing evidence for speciation with gene flow as a continuum between allopatric and sympatric extremes.
source: Today, allopatric and sympatric speciation are viewed as the two extremes on a multifaceted continuum of speciation with gene flow, for which there is growing evidence Foote, 2018; Richards et al., 2019.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Speciation with gene flow is generally assumed to start with divergent ecological selection.
source: Speciation with gene flow is generally assumed to start with divergent ecological selection, but for speciation to complete, additional components of reproductive isolation must come into play Smadja and Butlin, 2011; Seehausen et al., 2014.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Traits underlying ecological divergence and reproductive isolation must be genetically coupled to withstand gene flow and recombination.
source: Traits underlying ecological divergence and other components of reproductive isolation must be genetically coupled, as otherwise they cannot withstand the homogenizing effects of gene flow and recombination Smadja and Butlin, 2011; Felsenstein, 1981.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Genetic coupling can be achieved via pleiotropy, magic traits, or genetic linkage between respective genes.
source: Such coupling can be achieved via pleiotropy, magic traits, or genetic linkage between respective genes.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: Clunio marinus is found in the intertidal zone of the European Atlantic coast.
source: C. marinus is found in the intertidal zone of the European Atlantic coast.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about the species.

claim: Clunio marinus larvae live at the lower levels of the intertidal, which are almost permanently submerged.
source: Larvae live at the lower levels of the intertidal, which are almost permanently submerged.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about the species.

claim: Clunio marinus adults need the lower intertidal regions to be exposed by low tide for successful reproduction.
source: For successful reproduction, the adults need these regions to be exposed by the low tide.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about the species.

claim: The lowest tides predictably recur just after new moon and full moon.
source: The lowest tides predictably recur just after new moon and full moon.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about tidal patterns.

claim: Clunio marinus adults emerge only during full moon or new moon low tides, reproduce immediately and die a few hours later in the rising tide.
source: Therefore, C. marinus adults emerge only during full moon or new moon low tides, reproduce immediately and die a few hours later in the rising tide.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about the species' life cycle.

claim: The life cycle adaptation of Clunio marinus is based on a circalunar clock.
source: This life cycle adaptation is based on a circalunar clock, that is an endogenous time-keeping mechanism which synchronizes development and maturation with lunar phase.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about the species.

claim: Circalunar clocks are common in marine organisms, but their molecular basis is still unknown.
source: Circalunar clocks are common in marine organisms, but their molecular basis is still unknown Kaiser and Neumann, 2021.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: A circadian clock ensures that Clunio marinus adults only emerge during the low tide.
source: Additionally, a circadian clock ensures that C. marinus adults only emerge during the low tide Neumann, 1967.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Clunio marinus populations from different geographic sites show various genetic adaptations in circadian and circalunar timing.
source: As the pattern and amplitude of the tides differ dramatically along the coastline, C. marinus populations from different geographic sites show various genetic adaptations in circadian and circalunar timing Neumann, 1967; Kaiser, 2014; Kaiser et al., 2011.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Low tide water levels follow a bimodal distribution across a lunar month, with minima at both full moon and new moon.
source: Notably, low tide water levels follow a bimodal distribution across a lunar month, with minima at both full moon and new moon.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about tidal patterns.

claim: The minima at full moon and new moon are ecologically equally suitable for Clunio marinus reproduction, representing different timing niches.
source: These minima are ecologically equally suitable for C. marinus' reproduction, representing different timing niches that are occupied by different timing types (for details and definitions see Kaiser et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Some timing types of Clunio marinus use both timing niches (semi-lunar rhythm; SL type).
source: Some timing types of C. marinus use both niches ('semi-lunar rhythm'; SL type), but there are also dedicated full moon (FM) or new moon (NM) timing types, which occupy only one timing niche Kaiser et al., 2021.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: There are dedicated full moon (FM) or new moon (NM) timing types of Clunio marinus, which occupy only one timing niche.
source: Some timing types of C. marinus use both niches ('semi-lunar rhythm'; SL type), but there are also dedicated full moon (FM) or new moon (NM) timing types, which occupy only one timing niche Kaiser et al., 2021.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Water levels outside the minima are much less suitable for successful reproduction of Clunio marinus.
source: As water levels outside the minima are much less suitable for successful reproduction, we can expect divergent selection toward either full moon or new moon emergence.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an inference based on ecological conditions.

claim: Divergent selection toward either full moon or new moon emergence can be expected in Clunio marinus.
source: As water levels outside the minima are much less suitable for successful reproduction, we can expect divergent selection toward either full moon or new moon emergence.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an inference based on ecological conditions.

claim: Divergence into FM and NM timing types represents a magic trait because it automatically entails assortative mating.
source: This divergence into FM and NM timing types represents a magic trait, as it automatically entails assortative mating.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an inference based on the definition of magic traits.

claim: Hybrids between timing types are expected to emerge at intermediate times with respect to their parents.
source: Additionally, hybrids between timing types are expected to emerge at intermediate times with respect to their parents Neumann, 1967; Kaiser et al., 2011, that is during neap tide high tides.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Hybrids between timing types emerge during neap tide high tides.
source: Additionally, hybrids between timing types are expected to emerge at intermediate times with respect to their parents Neumann, 1967; Kaiser et al., 2011, that is during neap tide high tides.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Neap tide high tides are unfavorable for Clunio marinus reproduction.
source: As this tidal situation is unfavorable for C. marinus' reproduction, we can expect selection against hybrids, a form of an ecologically imposed postzygotic incompatibility.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an inference based on ecological conditions.

claim: Selection against hybrids is expected due to unfavorable tidal conditions, representing an ecologically imposed postzygotic incompatibility.
source: As this tidal situation is unfavorable for C. marinus' reproduction, we can expect selection against hybrids, a form of an ecologically imposed postzygotic incompatibility.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an inference based on ecological conditions.

claim: In Roscoff (France), FM and NM timing types occur in sympatry, largely separated by reproductive timing, but still connected by gene flow.
source: We recently discovered that in Roscoff (France) FM and NM timing types occur in sympatry, largely separated by reproductive timing, but still connected by gene flow Kaiser et al., 2021.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Polymorphic chromosomal inversions occur in all chromosome arms of the sympatric FM and NM types.
source: Here, we present evidence for polymorphic chromosomal inversions in all chromosome arms of the sympatric FM and NM types.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by data in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Quantitative trait loci (QTL) mapping for divergence in lunar reproductive timing identifies four unlinked and additive QTL in different chromosomes and inversions.
source: Quantitative trait loci (QTL) mapping for divergence in lunar reproductive timing identifies four unlinked and additive QTL in different chromosomes and inversions.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by QTL mapping data in Figure 5.

claim: Individual loci inside the inversions are more differentiated than the inversions themselves.
source: Individual loci inside the inversions are more differentiated than the inversions, suggesting that the inversions themselves are not directly required to maintain linkage disequilibrium between adaptive loci and that ecological divergence is kept up by permanent selection on unlinked loci on different chromosomes.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by FST data in Figure 5B.

claim: The inversions themselves are not directly required to maintain linkage disequilibrium between adaptive loci.
source: Individual loci inside the inversions are more differentiated than the inversions, suggesting that the inversions themselves are not directly required to maintain linkage disequilibrium between adaptive loci and that ecological divergence is kept up by permanent selection on unlinked loci on different chromosomes.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an inference based on differentiation patterns.

claim: Ecological divergence is kept up by permanent selection on unlinked loci on different chromosomes.
source: Individual loci inside the inversions are more differentiated than the inversions, suggesting that the inversions themselves are not directly required to maintain linkage disequilibrium between adaptive loci and that ecological divergence is kept up by permanent selection on unlinked loci on different chromosomes.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an inference based on the QTL mapping results.

claim: 48 individual genomes were sequenced for the FM and NM timing types (24 individuals each).
source: In order to gain insights into the loci and processes underlying sympatric divergence in reproductive timing, we sequenced 48 individual genomes for the FM and NM timing types (24 individuals each, defined by their lunar timing phenotype; genome size: 79.4 Mbp; average read coverage: 20 x).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the sequencing methods.

claim: The genome size of Clunio marinus is 79.4 Mbp.
source: In order to gain insights into the loci and processes underlying sympatric divergence in reproductive timing, we sequenced 48 individual genomes for the FM and NM timing types (24 individuals each, defined by their lunar timing phenotype; genome size: 79.4 Mbp; average read coverage: 20 x).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the sequencing data.

claim: The average read coverage for genome sequencing was 20x.
source: In order to gain insights into the loci and processes underlying sympatric divergence in reproductive timing, we sequenced 48 individual genomes for the FM and NM timing types (24 individuals each, defined by their lunar timing phenotype; genome size: 79.4 Mbp; average read coverage: 20 x).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the sequencing data.

claim: The sequencing resulted in a set of 721,000 genetic variants (608,599 SNPs; 112,401 small indels).
source: The resulting set of 721,000 genetic variants (608,599 SNPs; 112,401 small indels) indicated limited genetic differentiation between the FM and NM types (Figure 1; weighted genome-wide FST = 0.028).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the sequencing results.

claim: There is limited genetic differentiation between the FM and NM types with a weighted genome-wide FST of 0.028.
source: The resulting set of 721,000 genetic variants (608,599 SNPs; 112,401 small indels) indicated limited genetic differentiation between the FM and NM types (Figure 1; weighted genome-wide FST = 0.028).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Principal component analysis (PCA) and ADMIXTURE identify one individual as a migrant in time, which was caught at full moon among FM type individuals but genetically is of NM type.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) and ADMIXTURE identify one individual as a migrant in time, which was caught at full moon among FM type individuals, but genetically clearly is of NM type (Figure 1A and B; blue circle and arrow).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: Many individuals, particularly in the NM type, show ADMIXTURE fractions close to 0.5 or 0.25, suggesting they are F1 hybrids or backcrosses.
source: Many other individuals, particularly in the NM type, show ADMIXTURE fractions close to 0.5 or 0.25, suggesting they are F1 hybrids or backcrosses (Figure 1A and B; yellow circle and arrows).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: There are four FM individuals which are genetically distinct along principal component 2 and in ADMIXTURE at K=4.
source: Finally, there are four FM individuals, which are genetically distinct along principal component 2 and in ADMIXTURE at K=4 (Figure 1A and B; red circle and arrows).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: The four genetically distinct FM individuals might constitute either a sub-lineage of the FM type or migrants from a different geographic location.
source: These might constitute either a sub-lineage of the FM type or migrants from a different geographic location.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as speculation about the identity of these individuals.

claim: There is considerable hybridization of sympatric timing types and overall low genome-wide differentiation.
source: Taken together, full genome resequencing confirms that there is considerable hybridization of sympatric timing types and overall low genome-wide differentiation.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a summary of the genome sequencing findings.

claim: Chromosome 1 harbors a region of elevated FST that coincides with a block of long-range linkage-disequilibrium (LD) in the FM type.
source: Plotting genetic differentiation of the phenotypically defined FM and NM types along the genome (Figure 1C) revealed a region of elevated FST on the telocentric chromosome 1 (Figure 2A). This region coincides with a block of long-range linkage-disequilibrium (LD) in the FM type (Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Structural variant (SV) calling based on long-read sequencing data supports that the LD block on chromosome 1 represents a chromosomal inversion polymorphic in both timing types, called In(1a).
source: Structural variant (SV) calling based on additional long-read sequencing data supports that this block represents a chromosomal inversion polymorphic in both timing types, hereby called In(1a) (Figure 2C; full dataset in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The NM type shows a smaller LD block than the FM type, suggesting that a second structural variant occurs within the limits of the detected large chromosomal inversion.
source: Notably, the NM type shows a smaller LD block (Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggesting that a second structural variant occurs within the limits of the detected large chromosomal inversion.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Genetic linkage information obtained from crosses indicates that the second structural variant is a second inversion, named In(1b).
source: While this second variant was not picked up in SV calling, genetic linkage information obtained from crosses (described in detail below) indicates that this is a second inversion, named In(1b) (see double inverted marker order in Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by linkage mapping data in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Principal component analysis (PCA) for chromosomal sub-windows corresponding to suggested inversions separates individuals into clusters corresponding to standard haplotype homozygotes (SS), inversion homozygotes (I1I1, I2I2) and inversion heterozygotes (SI1, SI2, SI3, I1I2).
source: In a principal component analysis (PCA) on the genetic variants in these windows (Supplementary file 3), the four FM individuals that were already identified as genetically distinct (Figure 1) always cluster separately and cannot be assessed (Figure 2D-G, red question mark). The remaining 44 individuals are split into three genotype classes when PCA is performed on the non-overlapping regions of the large inversion (Figure 2D and F). These classes correspond to individuals homozygous for the standard haplotype (SS), individuals homozygous for an inverted haplotype (I1I1), and heterozygotes for the inversion (SI1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2D-G.

claim: Observed heterozygosity is clearly elevated in individuals heterozygous for the inversion.
source: Local observed heterozygosity is clearly elevated in individuals heterozygous for the inversion (Figure 2H and J), suggesting there are polymorphisms specific to the S or I1 haplotypes.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2H-K.

claim: There is substantial genetic differentiation between SS and I1I1 homozygotes, with FST values of up to 1.
source: This is corroborated by the patterns of genetic differentiation between SS and I1I1 homozygotes, which show FST values of up to 1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: In the region where both inversions overlap, the 44 individuals separate into six genotype clusters, corresponding to three clusters of inversion haplotype homozygotes (SS, I1I1, I2I2) and three clusters of heterozygotes (SI1, SI2, I1I2).
source: In the region where both inversions overlap (Figure 2E), the 44 individuals separate into six genotype clusters, corresponding to three clusters of inversion haplotype homozygotes (SS, I1I1, I2I2) and three clusters of heterozygotes (SI1, SI2, I1I2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The small inversion leading to haplotype I2 happened in the already inverted haplotype I1 of the large inversion.
source: This indicates that the small inversion leading to haplotype I2 happened in the already inverted haplotype I1 of the large inversion (compare Figure 2L).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2L.

claim: Sliding-window PCA analysis along the chromosomes confirms the patterns of segregation and the approximate genomic positions of inversion breakpoints.
source: A sliding-window PCA analysis along the chromosomes (500 kb windows, 100 kb steps; Figure 2—figure supplements 4–21) confirms these patterns of segregation and the approximate genomic positions of inversion breakpoints.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 4–21.

claim: There is a third inversion on chromosome 1, which ends at 24.8 Mbp, named In(1c).
source: Sliding-window PCA also indicated that there might be a third inversion, which ends at 24.8 Mbp (Figure 2A and G; Figure 2—figure supplements 4–21).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2A and G.

claim: The inversion leading to haplotype I3 happened in the standard haplotype S.
source: These three individuals are found in the SS cluster in the other genomic windows, implying that the inversion leading to haplotype I3 happened in the standard haplotype S (Figure 2L).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2L.

claim: Three inversion events are supported, named In(1a), In(1b) and In(1c), leading to four distinct haplotypes of chromosome 1 (S, I1, I2 and I3).
source: Taken together, our data support three inversion events, which we name In(1a), In(1b) and In(1c), leading to four distinct haplotypes of chromosome 1 (S, I1, I2 and I3; Figure 2L).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2L.

claim: The FM type carries all haplotypes but is dominated by the S haplotype.
source: The FM type carries all haplotypes but is dominated by the S haplotype, while the NM type almost exclusively carries the inverted I1 and I2 haplotypes.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2L.

claim: The NM type almost exclusively carries the inverted I1 and I2 haplotypes.
source: The FM type carries all haplotypes but is dominated by the S haplotype, while the NM type almost exclusively carries the inverted I1 and I2 haplotypes.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2L.

claim: The NM type shows recombination suppression only over the length of I2 because it is segregating almost exclusively for I1 and I2.
source: As the NM type is segregating almost exclusively for I1 and I2, it shows recombination suppression only over the length of I2.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference based on the haplotype distribution.

claim: The FM type shows recombination suppression along I1 because it is segregating for the S haplotype vs both I1 and I2.
source: The FM type is segregating for the S haplotype vs both I1 and I2, and thus shows recombination suppression along I1.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference based on the haplotype distribution.

claim: One putative chromosomal inversion is identified on each arm of the metacentric chromosomes 2 and 3, called In(2L), In(2R), In(3L) and In(3R).
source: The analysis of long-range LD also identifies one putative chromosomal inversion on each arm of the metacentric chromosomes 2 and 3 (Figure 3B and C; Figure 3—figure supplement 1). We call them In(2L), In(2R), In(3L) and In(3R).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: In(2L) is confirmed by inverted marker order in linkage mapping.
source: In(2L) is confirmed by inverted marker order in linkage mapping (Figure 5A and B) and In(2R) is confirmed by SV calling (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: In(2R) is confirmed by SV calling.
source: In(2L) is confirmed by inverted marker order in linkage mapping (Figure 5A and B) and In(2R) is confirmed by SV calling (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Supplementary file 1.

claim: Windowed PCA along the chromosomes confirms the approximate inversion breakpoints and allows genotyping of individuals for the inversion haplotypes.
source: As above, windowed PCA along the chromosomes confirms the approximate inversion breakpoints and allows to genotype the individuals for the inversion haplotypes (Figure 3D–G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3D-G.

claim: Heterozygosity is clearly elevated in inversion heterozygotes (SI) for inversions on chromosomes 2 and 3.
source: Heterozygosity is clearly elevated in inversion heterozygotes (SI; Figure 3H–K) and lowered in the inversion homozygotes (II; Figure 3H–K).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3H-K.

claim: Inversion homozygotes are absent for two of the inversions on chromosomes 2 and 3 and very rare for the other two.
source: Notably, inversion homozygotes are absent for two of these inversions (Figure 3D and F) and very rare for the other two (Figure 3E and G), suggesting these inversions might impose some fitness constraints.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3D-G.

claim: The inversions on chromosomes 2 and 3 might impose some fitness constraints.
source: Notably, inversion homozygotes are absent for two of these inversions (Figure 3D and F) and very rare for the other two (Figure 3E and G), suggesting these inversions might impose some fitness constraints.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as speculation based on the rarity of homozygotes.

claim: The four inversions on chromosomes 2 and 3 are only weakly differentiated between populations.
source: These four inversions are only weakly differentiated between populations (Figure 3L–O).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3L-O.

claim: Only In(2L) shows up as a block of mildly elevated genetic differentiation between the strains.
source: Only In(2L) shows up as a block of mildly elevated genetic differentiation between the strains (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: F1 hybrids between FM and NM types emerge at an intermediate time point between the FM and NM type emergence times, with a slight shift toward FM emergence.
source: F1 hybrids emerge at an intermediate time point between the FM and NM type emergence times, with a slight shift toward FM emergence (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In the F2 generation, the phenotype distribution is spread out but does not fully segregate into parental and F1 phenotype classes.
source: In the F2 generation, the phenotype distribution is spread out, but does not fully segregate into parental and F1 phenotype classes (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The difference in lunar reproductive timing is controlled by more than one genetic locus.
source: This indicates that the difference in lunar reproductive timing is controlled by more than one genetic locus.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference based on the F2 phenotype distribution.

claim: Genetic linkage mapping confirmed the existence of the inversions In(1a) and In(1b), both of which are supported by inverted marker order on the genetic linkage map.
source: Genetic linkage mapping confirmed the existence of the inversions In(1a) and In(1b), both of which are supported by inverted marker order on the genetic linkage map (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Marker order is inverted for In(2L) on the genetic linkage map.
source: Marker order is also inverted for In(2L), but not for the other inversions (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Stepwise QTL identification and Multiple QTL Mapping (MQM) found four largely additive QTL for the difference in lunar reproductive timing.
source: We then performed stepwise QTL identification and Multiple QTL Mapping (MQM) as implemented in R/qtl and found four largely additive QTL for the difference in lunar reproductive timing (Figure 5A and Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: A specific scan for epistatic effects only shows a weak interaction of chromosome 1 with the QTL on chromosome 2.
source: A specific scan for epistatic effects only shows a weak interaction of chromosome 1 with the QTL on chromosome 2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The four QTL model explains 54% of the total variance in lunar reproductive timing.
source: The four QTL model explains 54% of the total variance in lunar reproductive timing and the estimated additive effects of the QTL account for 6 days of the timing difference between the FM and NM type (Figure 5A, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 5A and Supplementary file 5.

claim: The estimated additive effects of the QTL account for 6 days of the timing difference between the FM and NM type.
source: The four QTL model explains 54% of the total variance in lunar reproductive timing and the estimated additive effects of the QTL account for 6 days of the timing difference between the FM and NM type (Figure 5A, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Supplementary file 5.

claim: The individual QTL explain 6.4%, 10.4%, 20.5%, and 10.8% of the variation in the phenotype.
source: The individual loci explain 6.4%, 10.4%, 20.5%, and 10.8% of the variation in the phenotype (Supplementary file 5), but given the size of our mapping family these values could be overestimated by approximately threefold King and Long, 2017 due to the Beavis effect Slate, 2013; Xu, 2003.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Supplementary file 5 and citations.

claim: The variance explained by individual QTL could be overestimated by approximately threefold due to the Beavis effect.
source: The individual loci explain 6.4%, 10.4%, 20.5%, and 10.8% of the variation in the phenotype (Supplementary file 5), but given the size of our mapping family these values could be overestimated by approximately threefold King and Long, 2017 due to the Beavis effect Slate, 2013; Xu, 2003.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: The actual variance explained by the QTL might be in the range of 2–7%.
source: This suggests that the actual variance explained by these loci might be rather in the range of 2–7% and that additional loci of smaller effects are likely to contribute to the phenotype.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference based on the Beavis effect.

claim: Additional loci of smaller effects are likely to contribute to the phenotype of lunar reproductive timing.
source: This suggests that the actual variance explained by these loci might be rather in the range of 2–7% and that additional loci of smaller effects are likely to contribute to the phenotype.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference based on the QTL mapping results.

claim: There are two QTL on chromosome 1, one of which overlaps with the inversion system.
source: There are two QTL on chromosome 1, one of which overlaps with the inversion system.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: The second QTL on chromosome 1 maps outside the inversion system and is well separated from the other QTL.
source: The second QTL on chromosome 1 maps outside the inversion system and is well separated from the other QTL (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: The QTL on chromosomes 2 and 3 overlap with In(2R) and In(3L), respectively.
source: The other two QTL are found on chromosomes 2 and 3 and overlap with In(2R) and In(3L), respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: The genomic regions underlying the QTL on chromosomes 2 and 3 are large and show several peaks in genetic differentiation.
source: The genomic regions underlying these QTL are large and show several peaks in genetic differentiation (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The QTL on chromosome 2 and 3 possibly harbor a set of linked loci influencing the lunar emergence phenotype.
source: Possibly, the QTL on chromosome 2 and 3 harbor a set of linked loci influencing the lunar emergence phenotype.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as speculation based on the multiple differentiation peaks.

claim: There are at least four unlinked loci which influence the magic trait of lunar reproductive timing.
source: Taken together, there are at least four unlinked loci which influence this magic trait.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a summary of the QTL mapping findings.

claim: The overall genetic architecture of lunar reproductive timing in the populations may be even more complex than described, given that the QTL mapping was based on a single pair of parents.
source: Given that the QTL mapping was based on a single pair of parents, the overall genetic architecture in the populations may be even more complex than what we described here.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as speculation about the limitations of the study.

claim: In all chromosomal inversions there are loci that are far more differentiated than the inversion itself.
source: While some chromosomal inversions show up as genetically differentiated blocks, in all chromosomal inversions there are loci that are far more differentiated than the inversion itself (compare Figure 2L and Figure 3L to O with Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figures 2L, 3L-O, and 5B.

claim: The inversions are not required for protecting genetic differentiation.
source: This implies that the inversions are not required for protecting genetic differentiation.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference based on differentiation patterns.

claim: An insertion-deletion (indel) mutation was identified in the highly differentiated first intron of the period gene.
source: We identified an insertion-deletion (indel) mutation in the highly differentiated first intron of the period gene (Figure 5C, green arrows) and re-genotyped the 48 individuals for this indel (Figure 5D; Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Period alleles are strongly differentiated between the FM and NM types.
source: This confirmed that period alleles are indeed strongly differentiated between the FM and NM types.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Period alleles are not closely associated with the inversion haplotypes of chromosome 1.
source: However, we could not find a close association between the period alleles and the inversion haplotypes of chromosome 1 (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Both period alleles occur in several inversion haplotypes, confirming that there is gene flux between standard and inversion haplotypes.
source: Both alleles occur is several inversion haplotypes, confirming that there is gene flux between standard and inversion haplotypes.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Differentiation of the period locus is not driven by differentiation of the inversion system.
source: This implies that differentiation of the period locus is not driven by differentiation of the inversion system, that is it is not enhanced by LD with other locally adaptive variants.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference based on the lack of association between period alleles and inversion haplotypes.

claim: The period locus is the most differentiated locus within the QTL in the inversion system on chromosome 1.
source: The QTL in the inversion system on chromosome 1 is narrow and harbors a single strongly divergent locus, which is the period locus (Figure 5B, red asterisk). The period locus is the most differentiated locus in the entire genome (maximum FST = 0.86) and period is a core circadian clock gene.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The period locus has a maximum FST of 0.86.
source: The period locus is the most differentiated locus in the entire genome (maximum FST = 0.86) and period is a core circadian clock gene.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: Period is a core circadian clock gene.
source: The period locus is the most differentiated locus in the entire genome (maximum FST = 0.86) and period is a core circadian clock gene.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as established knowledge.

claim: The QTL at the end of chromosome 1, outside the inversion system, shows a single strong divergence peak at the first intron of the plum gene.
source: The QTL at the end of chromosome 1, outside the inversion system, also shows a single strong divergence peak (Figure 5B, red circle). This is the first intron of the plum gene (Figure 5—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 5.

claim: The large intron of the plum gene likely contains regulatory regions for both plum and the directly adjacent cask gene.
source: The large intron likely contains regulatory regions for both plum and the directly adjacent cask gene.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference based on genomic structure.

claim: On chromosome arm 2R the QTL has several divergence peaks, but the strongest peak hits the stat1 gene.
source: On chromosome arm 2R the QTL has several divergence peaks, but the strongest peak hits the stat1 gene (Figure 5B, red plus sign; Figure 5—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 6.

claim: Plum, cask, and stat1 are all involved in nervous system development in Drosophila melanogaster.
source: Plum, cask, and stat1 are all involved in nervous system development in Drosophila melanogaster Yu et al., 2013; Gillespie and Hodge, 2013; Ngo et al., 2010, suggesting that divergence in lunar reproductive timing may involve nervous system remodeling as well as circadian timekeeping.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: Divergence in lunar reproductive timing may involve nervous system remodeling as well as circadian timekeeping.
source: Plum, cask, and stat1 are all involved in nervous system development in Drosophila melanogaster Yu et al., 2013; Gillespie and Hodge, 2013; Ngo et al., 2010, suggesting that divergence in lunar reproductive timing may involve nervous system remodeling as well as circadian timekeeping.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference based on gene functions.

claim: Evidence from gene function, genetic divergence and QTL mapping align to support period, plum, cask, and stat1 as candidate genes.
source: These gene functions are plausible to be involved in lunar time-keeping and congruent with the results from a companion study Fuhrmann et al., 2023, which assessed the loss of lunar timing in a different set of Clunio populations. Thus, evidence from gene function, genetic divergence and QTL mapping align to support these candidate genes.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a summary of the candidate gene evidence.

claim: Multiple large and polymorphic chromosomal inversions were found in the sympatric FM and NM strains, covering all chromosome arms of the C. marinus genome.
source: We found multiple large and polymorphic chromosomal inversions in the sympatric FM and NM strains, covering all chromosome arms of the C. marinus genome.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of findings.

claim: The inversions found are consistent with large non-pairing and inverted regions observed in C. marinus polytene chromosomes.
source: This is consistent with large non-pairing and inverted regions observed in C. marinus polytene chromsomes Michailova, 1980.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: The inversions reduce recombination, as is observed in large LD blocks.
source: These inversions reduce recombination, as is observed in large LD blocks (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1), and possibly lock several loci involved in divergent reproductive timing into supergenes (Figures 2A and 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The inversions possibly lock several loci involved in divergent reproductive timing into supergenes.
source: These inversions reduce recombination, as is observed in large LD blocks (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1), and possibly lock several loci involved in divergent reproductive timing into supergenes (Figures 2A and 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as speculation based on the inversion patterns.

claim: Most of the inversions are not differentiated between timing types.
source: However, most of these inversions are not differentiated between timing types and in all inversions, there are loci more divergent than the inversion itself.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of findings.

claim: Divergent alleles at the period locus are not associated with specific inversion haplotypes or the standard haplotype.
source: We show that divergent alleles at the period locus are not associated with specific inversion haplotypes or the standard haplotype (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and shown in Figure 5D.

claim: There must be considerable recombination and/or gene conversion inside the inversion, placing the period alleles in different inversion haplotypes.
source: Thus, there must be considerable recombination and/or gene conversion inside the inversion, placing the period alleles in different inversion haplotypes.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an inference based on the lack of association between period alleles and inversion haplotypes.

claim: Genetic linkage is not the major mechanism for coupling ecological divergence and assortative mating in this study system.
source: We therefore propose that in this study system genetic linkage is not the major mechanism for coupling ecological divergence and assortative mating.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion based on the findings.

claim: The magic trait scenario is favored, in which recombination does not matter because the relevant components of reproductive isolation are influenced by a single trait.
source: Instead, we favor the magic trait scenario, in which recombination does not matter, because the relevant components of reproductive isolation are influenced by a single trait.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion based on the findings.

claim: All loci influencing the magic trait will be under divergent natural selection.
source: Given a magic trait, all loci influencing the trait will be under divergent natural selection.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an inference based on the magic trait concept.

claim: Peaks of genetic differentiation include the loci responsible for ecological adaptation, and their differentiation is driven by permanent divergent natural selection.
source: We thus assume that peaks of genetic differentiation include the loci responsible for ecological adaptation, and that their differentiation is driven by permanent divergent natural selection.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an inference based on the magic trait scenario.

claim: Physical linkage between adaptive alleles and inversion haplotypes, though incomplete, may drive the spread of specific inversion haplotypes and thus differentiation of the inversion system on chromosome 1.
source: As a consequence, physical linkage between adaptive alleles and inversion haplotypes, though incomplete, may drive the spread of specific inversion haplotypes and thus differentiation of the inversion system on chromosome 1.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as speculation about the evolutionary dynamics.

claim: Differentiation of the inversion system creates a genetic substrate for further components of reproductive isolation to evolve and be genetically linked to the existing loci responsible for reproductive isolation.
source: Differentiation of the inversion system then creates a genetic substrate for further components of reproductive isolation to evolve and be genetically linked to the existing loci responsible for reproductive isolation.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as speculation about future evolutionary trajectories.

claim: Eventually, the differentiation of the inversion system may lead to the completion of speciation.
source: Eventually, this may lead to the completion of speciation.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as speculation about future evolutionary outcomes.

claim: The study is not dealing with a single pleiotropic locus that affects several components of reproductive isolation.
source: At the same time, QTL mapping revealed at least four independent loci underlying lunar reproductive timing. Therefore, we are neither dealing with a single pleiotropic locus that affects several components of reproductive isolation, nor with a single supergene that would combine genetic variants underlying different components of reproductive isolation, such as local adaptation and assortative mating.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion based on the QTL mapping results.

claim: The study is not dealing with a single supergene that would combine genetic variants underlying different components of reproductive isolation.
source: At the same time, QTL mapping revealed at least four independent loci underlying lunar reproductive timing. Therefore, we are neither dealing with a single pleiotropic locus that affects several components of reproductive isolation, nor with a single supergene that would combine genetic variants underlying different components of reproductive isolation, such as local adaptation and assortative mating.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion based on the QTL mapping results.

claim: An oligogenic architecture can underlie ecological and reproductive divergence in sympatric populations.
source: Our data show that an oligogenic architecture can underlie ecological and reproductive divergence in sympatric populations.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion based on the findings.

claim: The four QTL identified for the difference in lunar reproductive timing between the FM and NM types in Roscoff do not overlap with the two QTL identified previously for difference in lunar reproductive timing between Normandy (Por-1SL) and Basque Coast (Jean-2NM) strains.
source: In addition, the four QTL we identified here for the difference in lunar reproductive timing between the FM and NM types in Roscoff do not overlap with the two QTL we identified previously for difference in lunar reproductive timing between Normandy (Por-1SL) and Basque Coast (Jean-2NM) strains Kaiser et al., 2016; Kaiser and Heckel, 2012.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: Within the species C. marinus, different populations have found different genetic solutions for adapting lunar reproductive timing to the local tidal regime.
source: This indicates that within the species C. marinus, different populations have found different genetic solutions for adapting lunar reproductive timing to the local tidal regime.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an inference based on the comparison of QTL across populations.

claim: The overall genetic basis of lunar reproductive timing may be even more complex than shown, given that both studies relied on a single crossing family.
source: Given that both studies relied on a single crossing family, the overall genetic basis of lunar reproductive timing may even be more complex than what we have shown here.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as speculation about the limitations of the study.

claim: During the last ice age, the English Channel did not exist, setting the time frame of establishment of the sympatric Roscoff populations roughly to the last 10,000 years.
source: During the last ice age, the English Channel did not exist Patton et al., 2017, setting the time frame of establishment of the sympatric Roscoff populations roughly to the last 10,000 years.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: Genetic differentiation between the inversion haplotypes is higher than what would be expected to evolve in the last 10,000 years.
source: Genetic differentiation between the inversion haplotypes (Figure 2—figure supplement 3) is higher than what would be expected to evolve in this time-frame.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The inversions were already segregating in the ancestral populations or may have recently introgressed from a different geographic site.
source: We thus assume that the inversions were already segregating in the ancestral populations or may have recently introgressed from a different geographic site.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as speculation based on the high differentiation of inversions.

claim: The genetic variants underlying sympatric ecological divergence might have introgressed from a different geographic site.
source: The latter might also be true for the genetic variants underlying sympatric ecological divergence.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as speculation.

claim: The detection of period as the most differentiated locus between NM and FM types, overlapping with a QTL for lunar reproductive timing, suggests that this circadian clock gene might also be involved in lunar time-keeping.
source: The detection of period as the most differentiated locus between NM and FM types, overlapping with a QTL for lunar reproductive timing, suggests that this circadian clock gene might also be involved in lunar time-keeping.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an inference based on the findings.

claim: Plum, cask, and stat1 are involved in neuronal or synaptic development and plasticity.
source: The other prominent candidates, plum, cask, and stat1 are involved in neuronal or synaptic development and plasticity.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as established knowledge.

claim: Cask is a direct interaction partner of CaMKII.
source: Notably, cask is a direct interaction partner of CaMKII Gillespie and Hodge, 2013, which we previously found to be involved in circadian timing differences in Clunio Kaiser et al., 2016.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: CaMKII was previously found to be involved in circadian timing differences in Clunio.
source: Notably, cask is a direct interaction partner of CaMKII Gillespie and Hodge, 2013, which we previously found to be involved in circadian timing differences in Clunio Kaiser et al., 2016.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: Both QTL on chromosome 1 suggest a close connection of circadian and circalunar time-keeping.
source: Hence, both QTL on chromosome 1 suggest a close connection of circadian and circalunar time-keeping.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an inference based on the candidate genes.

claim: Genomic analysis of the loss of lunar rhythms in Baltic and Arctic Clunio strains implied circadian GO terms as the top candidates for affecting circalunar time-keeping, followed by GO terms involved in nervous system development.
source: This is backed by recent findings in Baltic and Arctic Clunio strains, for which genomic analysis of the loss of lunar rhythms also implied circadian GO terms as the top candidates for affecting circalunar time-keeping, followed by GO terms involved in nervous system development Fuhrmann et al., 2023.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: The data elucidate the genetic architecture underlying a magic trait.
source: Thus, our data not only elucidate the genetic architecture underlying a magic trait, but also give hints to the genetic basis of the yet enigmatic circalunar clock.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of the study's contributions.

claim: The data give hints to the genetic basis of the yet enigmatic circalunar clock.
source: Thus, our data not only elucidate the genetic architecture underlying a magic trait, but also give hints to the genetic basis of the yet enigmatic circalunar clock.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of the study's contributions.
